patient_information: A 35-year-old Peruvian man with a past medical history of hepatitis of unknown etiology 20 years prior. He had not received any vaccinations since his early childhood.
chief_complaint: Fever, retro-orbital headache, jaundice, bleeding, and altered mental status for eight days.
history_of_present_illness: The illness began eight days prior to presentation with fever and retro-orbital headache. Two days into the illness, he developed jaundice, coffee-ground vomiting, gross haematuria, and increasing mental obtundation, leading to admission at a local hospital in the jungle. During transfer to the referral hospital in Lima, he experienced a generalized seizure.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient worked as a logging supervisor for the past 5 years in a remote jungle area near Pucallpa, Peru, on the shores of the Ucayali River. This occupation created possible contact with sylvatic mosquitoes and animals. He reported not taking any malaria prophylaxis.
vitals: On admission, his temperature was 38.8°C, blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg, heart rate was 110 beats per minute, and respiratory rate was 24 breaths per minute.
physical_exam: The patient was agitated, unresponsive to verbal commands, and intermittently stuporous. He was jaundiced, with spontaneous bleeding from his oral mucosa and at venipuncture sites, and had multiple large ecchymoses on his face, trunk, and limbs. Neurological examination revealed a marked flapping of hands (asterixis) with no focal or meningeal signs. Lung auscultation revealed crepitant rales in both bases. The liver was felt 3 cm below the right costal margin, while the spleen was not palpable and there was no lymphadenopathy.
labs_and_diagnostics: Initial labs showed anaemia (haematocrit 30%), thrombocytopenia (platelets 110,000/μL), severe transaminitis (AST 2890 U/L, ALT 2676 U/L), hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 11.6 mg/dL), and coagulopathy (INR 2.6, aPTT 80 s). Urinalysis showed proteinuria and hematuria. Three malaria thick films were negative, as were blood cultures and serologies for Brucella and Hepatitis B (IgM anti-Hbc). The diagnosis was confirmed by a highly positive IgM capture ELISA for yellow fever at a 1:10000 titer. Anti-dengue IgM was negative. A chest x-ray eventually showed bilateral pulmonary infiltrates compatible with ARDS.
differential_diagnosis: The differential diagnosis for this acute febrile illness with liver failure included severe malaria, though the transaminases were exceptionally high. Other considerations were viral hepatitis (A, B, C, D, E), toxin-mediated hepatitis, leptospirosis, typhoid fever, and brucellosis. Severe dengue was less likely due to the prolonged fever and low hematocrit. Given his occupation, jungle exposure, and unvaccinated status, a viral haemorrhagic fever, particularly yellow fever, was highly suspected.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient received presumptive treatment for malaria, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and supportive care. Over the subsequent three days, his condition worsened with increasing hepatic encephalopathy, renal failure (creatinine 6.5 mg/dL), coma, and disseminated intravascular coagulation with severe bleeding. He developed ARDS confirmed by chest x-ray. His liver transaminases dropped suddenly on day 3, indicating acute hepatic disintegration. The patient died one day later.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis was Yellow Fever. This was based on the clinical presentation of fever, jaundice, bleeding, and multi-organ failure in an unvaccinated individual with significant occupational exposure as a logger in an endemic region of Peru. The diagnosis was confirmed serologically by a highly positive IgM capture ELISA for yellow fever (1:10000). Alternative diagnoses such as malaria, bacterial sepsis, hepatitis B, and dengue were ruled out by negative laboratory investigations.
